claims.claim: The name Oecumenius represents in the present state of investigation a riddle that can be solved only by thorough critical study of the manuscripts in connexion with the whole question of the Catenae.
The compiler of the commentary on the Pauline epistles is in fact unknown, and the historical Oecumenius, the sixth-century commentator on the Apocalypse, is a different writer.
Migne prints the commentary under the name of Oecumenius, bishop of Tricca, a convention going back to the 1532 editio princeps.
Manuscripts of the eleventh century contain commentaries on the Pauline epistles attributed since the sixteenth century to Oecumenius.
The first manuscripts of the Pauline commentaries are older than Theophylact, so that it cannot be merely a false attribution of his work.
Among the authors quoted in the Pauline commentaries, the name of Oecumenius itself occurs repeatedly.
Oecumenius is cited very often in a manuscript Catena in Epistolas Pauli formerly in the Coislinian library at Paris, which Montfaucon ascribes to the tenth century.
In a manuscript cited by Montfaucon, Oecumenius is styled bishop of Tricca in Thessaly.
